extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent agents and patent attorneys), USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline, patent practice managers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria the USPTO uses to assess practitioner conduct in disciplinary proceedings, especially regarding certifications of micro entity status, obligations to inquire, and firm procedure adequacy. Includes aggravating/mitigating factors and typical sanctions and publication practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry before presenting certifications (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Must conduct a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances prior to presenting certifications (e.g., Certifications of Micro Entity Status) to the USPTO, particularly where the USPTO will rely on those certifications regarding application filing limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order describes the obligation as 'not always conducting a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 prior to presenting certifications of micro entity status to the USPTO ...' Examples of obstacles to inquiry (not excuses) include Romanization of names, language barriers, or applicants' deceptive intent. The practitioner remains responsible to perform a reasonable inquiry when certifying facts that the Office will rely upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence in representing a client; failure to do so (including not conducting reasonable inquiry and lacking adequate procedures) violates § 11.103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order finds violation by 'not always conducting a reasonable inquiry ... and failing to have had in place adequate procedures to ensure that every certification of micro entity status complies with USPTO regulations.' Diligence encompasses both individual inquiry and establishing firm systems to prevent recurring errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice (e.g., presenting unreliable certifications to the USPTO) violates § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order treats presenting certifications without reasonable inquiry or adequate procedures as potentially 'prejudicial to the administration of justice.' The same factual failures supporting a diligence violation can also violate § 11.804(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity certification compliance (37 C.F.R. § 1.29(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Certifications of Micro Entity Status must accurately reflect statutory/regulatory eligibility, including the micro entity application filing limit (e.g., that 'neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has been named as the inventor or a joint inventor on more than four previously filed U.S. patent applications').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noting that Notices of Additional Fees Due were issued where 'the micro entity application filing limit was exceeded,' the Order emphasizes the practitioner's obligation to ensure accuracy before certifying. Practitioners must verify prior application counts and related ownership/assignment facts before signing micro entity certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility of the attorney/agent of record for certifications signed
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney or agent of record who signs and files a certification (e.g., Certification of Micro Entity Status) is responsible for ensuring it complies with USPTO regulations and for the consequences of incorrect certifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order references that Respondent, as attorney of record, signed Certifications of Micro Entity Status and that the USPTO would rely on those certifications regarding the application filing limit. Signing signifies responsibility even where external factors (language, Romanization) complicated verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain adequate firm procedures and docketing systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms and practitioners must have adequate procedures (including docketing systems and conflict checks) to ensure certifications and filings comply with USPTO rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order indicates failures were 'in large part, due to his firm's insufficient docketing system' and cites the practitioner's later adoption of measures (master spreadsheet with exemplary figures, identification card info, inventor info, search keywords; modified declaration forms; more meetings and outside presentations regarding conflict checks) as corrective measures. Adequate procedures are both a compliance obligation and a mitigating factor when implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify applicant identity and prior applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must take steps to corroborate applicant/inventor identity and to ascertain prior patent application history before certifying statuses that depend on those facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order explains difficulties due to 'the Romanization of an inventor's name' and the respondent's 'non-native language limitations,' and notes the modified declaration form now asks inventors to sign names in native language and English and list all prior patent applications. Such verification practices are recommended to prevent erroneous certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt corrective action upon notice (change entity status and pay deficiency fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: When notified by the USPTO of apparent errors (e.g., Notices of Additional Fees Due), practitioners should timely correct entity status and pay any deficiency fees on active applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order records that Respondent 'timely changed the entity status and paid the deficiency fee on all the applications that remained active' and that he proactively identified and corrected other erroneous certifications. Taking prompt remedial action is a factual point the OED considers favorably in sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors the Office considers in sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office considers lack of prior disciplinary history, acknowledgment of lapses, genuine contrition, full cooperation with investigation, proactive corrective action, and adoption of measures to prevent recurrence as mitigating factors when determining discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order explicitly lists (i) no prior discipline; (ii) acknowledgement and contrition; (iii) full cooperation and supplemental responses; (iv) sua sponte corrective action (changing entity status and paying deficiency fees); and (v) adoption of preventive measures as factors leading to a public reprimand rather than harsher sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, publication, and notice practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible sanctions include public reprimand and publication of the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and a notice in the Official Gazette that is materially consistent with the specified language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order directs: (a) public reprimand; (b) electronic publication in the OED FOIA Reading Room; and (c) publication of a notice in the Official Gazette with materially consistent notice text. The sample notice summarizes violations, factual context, and mitigating factors and is used as the model for public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disciplinary record in future proceedings (aggravating factor/rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disciplinary record (including the Final Order) may be considered in future complaints or proceedings against the practitioner, either as an aggravating factor or to rebut statements by the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order states the Office may consider the record: (1) when addressing further complaints of the same or similar misconduct, and (2) in future disciplinary proceedings as an aggravating factor in determining discipline and/or to rebut statements by or on behalf of the respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement terms may include waiver of review and appeal rights
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of a settlement, a practitioner may agree to waive rights to seek reconsideration (37 C.F.R. § 11.56), review (37 C.F.R. § 11.57), or otherwise appeal or challenge the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order records Respondent's agreement to waive all rights to seek reconsideration and review and to waive appeal, which is a common settlement term that finalizes discipline and limits further procedural challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of costs in settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The settlement may provide that each party shall bear its own costs incurred to date and in carrying out the settlement terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (f) of the Agreed-Upon Sanction states 'The parties shall bear their own costs incurred to date and in carrying out the terms of the Proposed Settlement Agreement and this Final Order.' Cost allocation is therefore a negotiable element of resolution.
